"**Kill This Love**" is a song recorded by South Korean girl group [Blackpink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpink "Blackpink"). It was released on April 4, 2019, through [YG Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YG_Entertainment "YG Entertainment") and [Interscope Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interscope_Records "Interscope Records"), as the lead single for the group's second Korean extended play of the [same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love "Kill This Love"). The Japanese version of the single was released through [Universal Music Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Japan "Universal Music Japan") on October 16, 2019\. It was written by [Teddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Park "Teddy Park") and [Bekuh Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekuh_Boom "Bekuh Boom") and produced by them alongside [R. Tee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Tee "R. Tee") and 24\. The single has been described as an [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop") song, whose lyrics talk about the girls' decision to end a toxic relationship.

Commercially, "Kill This Love" peaked at number two on the [Gaon Digital Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaon_Digital_Chart "Gaon Digital Chart") and the *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* [K-pop Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop_Hot_100 "K-pop Hot 100") in South Korea. The song became the group's first top-50 hit on the US [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") and the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"), thus also becoming the highest-charting song by a female K-pop act on both charts. It reached number one in Malaysia as well as on *Billboard* [World Digital Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Digital_Songs "World Digital Songs"), and entered the national charts in 27 countries. The song has been certified double diamond in Brazil, platinum in South Korea, Japan, Australia, France, and New Zealand, and silver in the United Kingdom, among others.

An accompanying music video for the song was directed by Seo Hyun-seung and uploaded onto Blackpink's [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel simultaneously with the single's release. Upon release, it broke the record for the most-viewed music video within 24 hours, accumulating 56\.7 million views in that time. It has since become the second music video by a K-pop group to reach two billion views after "[Ddu-Du Ddu-Du](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du")" (2018), making Blackpink the first K-pop act in history to have two videos reach the milestone. It also became one of [the most-liked videos on YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most-liked_YouTube_videos "List of most-liked YouTube videos") with over 25 million likes on the platform, and won the [Music Video of 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Choice_Award_for_Favorite_Music_Video "People's Choice Award for Favorite Music Video") award at the [45th People's Choice Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45th_People's_Choice_Awards "45th People's Choice Awards").

## Background and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love_\(song\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

[Yang Hyun-suk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Hyun-suk "Yang Hyun-suk"), then-CEO of [YG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YG_Entertainment "YG Entertainment") announced on February 8, 2019, that Blackpink was set for a comeback with an EP in March.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) The single and EP were announced on March 25\.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) Between March 31 and April 1, multiple individual teaser pictures were posted onto their social media accounts.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) On July 26, it was announced that the group would release a Japanese version of their EP *Kill This Love* on September 11, 2019\.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) The album missed its initial release date and was released on October 16, 2019\. No song of the version was released as a single.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) A live recording of the Japanese version of "Kill This Love", recorded in the [Tokyo Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Dome "Tokyo Dome") on December 4, 2019, was included in the group's third live album *Blackpink 2019–2020 World Tour In Your Area – Tokyo Dome*, released on May 6, 2020, through [Universal Music Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Universal_Music_Group_labels#Universal_Music_Japan "List of Universal Music Group labels").[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)

The song was written by [Teddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Park "Teddy Park") and [Bekuh Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekuh_Boom "Bekuh Boom"), who previously wrote "[Ddu-Du Ddu-Du](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du")", while production was handled by them alongside [R. Tee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Tee "R. Tee") and 24\. Its lyrics have been described as a "breakup anthem"[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) and the song itself has been described as a stomping, brassy electropop track with trap elements.[\[8\]](#cite_note-BlackpinkMV-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-9) The song contains "blaring horns and martial percussion",[\[10\]](#cite_note-:0-10) with [Rosé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosé_\(singer\) "Rosé (singer)") and [Jisoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jisoo_\(singer,_born_1995\) "Jisoo (singer, born 1995)") leading the "impassioned" pre-choruses about breaking up.[\[10\]](#cite_note-:0-10) The song ends with an "imperial rallying cry to cut off the dead weight".[\[10\]](#cite_note-:0-10)

## Critical reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love_\(song\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Critical reception")\]

"Kill This Love" received mixed reviews from music critics. Erica Russell from *[Paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_\(magazine\) "Paper (magazine)")* gave a glowing review, ranking "Kill This Love" as the best song of 2019 and praised it as a "perfect" sonic blend of all the group members and an "explosive culmination" of the musical trends that dominated the past decade.[\[11\]](#cite_note-Paper-11) J.M.K from *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* ranked it 25th on their list of the best K-pop songs of 2019, remarking that the group's "girl crush' concept never felt more visceral".[\[12\]](#cite_note-BBJMK-12) In another *Billboard* article, staff writer Andrew Unterberger placed the song 66th in the year's best songs and described the production as "practically biblical".[\[13\]](#cite_note-BBAU-13) Yannik Gölz from *[Laut.de](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laut.de "Laut.de")* regarded the track as a "sensory overload" and felt that it "delivers everything you would want from Blackpink". He characterized it as "spectacular, cartoon-like and overdrawn trap-pop packed to the point of irritation", but also expressed a desire for a more suitable hook.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)

Conversely, Michelle Kim from *[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)")* gave it an unfavorable review, describing the song's production as strangely out of date and suggesting it could have been produced in the early 2010s. She drew parallels between the song and [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift")'s 2015 single "[Bad Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Blood_\(Taylor_Swift_song\) "Bad Blood (Taylor Swift song)")", albeit without a "catchy Swiftian hook".[\[9\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-9) Rhian Daly from *[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")* expressed disappointment with the track's production, labelling the chorus as uninspiring and a letdown following the song's initial buildup.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) Nur Izzaty Shaifullizan from *[The Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star_\(Malaysia\) "The Star (Malaysia)")* made comparisons to the group's 2018 hit "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" and felt that it was hardly an improvement.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

## Commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love_\(song\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Commercial performance")\]

In South Korea "Kill This Love" debuted at number 25 on the [Gaon Digital Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaon_Digital_Chart "Gaon Digital Chart") with only one and a half days of charting, later peaking at number two the second week, giving the group their sixth top five song.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Gaon-23) In the United States, the single debuted at number 41 on the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") to become the highest-charting Hot 100 hit ever by a K-pop girl group. The song debuted at number 22 on the [Streaming Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_Songs "Streaming Songs") chart with 18\.6 million streams and rose 48–39 on the [Digital Song Sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Song_Sales "Digital Song Sales") chart with 7,000 downloads sold.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24) The song stayed in the Hot 100 for a total of four consecutive weeks, making it the longest-charting song by an all-female Korean act on the chart.[\[25\]](#cite_note-25) In the United Kingdom, "Kill This Love" charted at number 33, the highest for any female Korean act at the time.[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) In May 2021, the song was certified silver by the [British Phonographic Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Phonographic_Industry "British Phonographic Industry") (BPI) for moving 200,000 [single-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit"), the group's first solo single to do so.[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) The track reached 43\.1 million streams in the UK as of September 2022, becoming the group's second most streamed song in the country.[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) In 2026, "Kill This Love" surpassed 1 billion streams on [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify"),[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) making Blackpink the first female K-pop act to have multiple songs exceed the milestone following "[How You Like That](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_You_Like_That "How You Like That")" (2020).[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)

## Music video

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love_\(song\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Music video")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/56/Rose_-_Kill_This_Love.jpg/250px-Rose_-_Kill_This_Love.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rose_-_Kill_This_Love.jpg)

[KBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Broadcasting_System "Korean Broadcasting System") banned the music video as member [Rosé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosé_\(singer\) "Rosé (singer)") is seen driving a car without a seatbelt.

An accompanying music video for the song was directed by Seo Hyun-seung and shot in mid-March, and was released on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") simultaneously with the song.[\[42\]](#cite_note-43)[\[43\]](#cite_note-44) According to *Billboard*, the visual features a variety of weapons, ranging from a car being driven with an intent to kill, to a giant hunting trap. The music video also features elements of [Greek mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology"), such as the fractured [Aphrodite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodite "Aphrodite") statue serving as a metaphor for broken love, and features references to [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") regarding the ecclesiastical setting.[\[8\]](#cite_note-BlackpinkMV-8)

Upon the music video's release, "Kill This Love" broke the record of the fastest video to reach 1 million likes in just 28 minutes.[\[44\]](#cite_note-45) It earned the biggest music video debut in YouTube history with 56\.7 million views within 24 hours of release, surpassing the record held by [Ariana Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariana_Grande "Ariana Grande")'s "[Thank U, Next](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thank_U,_Next_\(song\) "Thank U, Next (song)")" (2018).[\[45\]](#cite_note-records-46) Furthermore, it became the fastest video to reach 100 million views on YouTube, doing so in approximately 2 days and 14 hours, beating the record set by fellow Korean artist [Psy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psy "Psy") with "[Gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentleman_\(Psy_song\) "Gentleman (Psy song)")" in 2013\.[\[46\]](#cite_note-47)[\[45\]](#cite_note-records-46) It also set the record for the biggest YouTube premiere with 979,000 concurrent viewers.[\[47\]](#cite_note-48) "Kill This Love" surpassed two billion views in September 2024, marking the group's second video to hit the milestone after "[Ddu-Du Ddu-Du](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du")".[\[48\]](#cite_note-49)

On April 9, 2019, the dance practice video for "Kill This Love" was released on Blackpink's official YouTube channel.[\[49\]](#cite_note-50) South Korean public broadcaster [KBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Broadcasting_System "Korean Broadcasting System") banned the music video "for violating the country's Road Traffic Act", due to a scene in which [Rosé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosé_\(singer\) "Rosé (singer)") is seen driving a car at high speed without a [seatbelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seat_belt "Seat belt").[\[50\]](#cite_note-51)

## Live performances

On January 31, 2021, the group performed "Kill This Love" as the opening number of their virtual concert [The Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Show_\(concert\) "The Show (concert)").[\[55\]](#cite_note-56) *Billboard* praised the reworking of the song with a live band accompanying them and deemed it one of the standout moments of the show.[\[56\]](#cite_note-57) Blackpink also included the song on the setlist of their second worldwide concert tour, the [Born Pink World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born_Pink_World_Tour "Born Pink World Tour") (2022–2023).[\[57\]](#cite_note-58) In April and June 2023, they performed "Kill This Love" during their headlining sets at Coachella and [BST Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BST_Hyde_Park "BST Hyde Park") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London").[\[58\]](#cite_note-59)[\[59\]](#cite_note-60)

import re, math, json, os, urllib.request

    lv = parsed[-1]  # highest resolution
